coverage.note: Bounded P01 migration. Whole-outline rebuild remains blocked until product-complete substrate exists.

world.operation: record and authenticate administrative information through several coexisting clay-based practices

records.statement: Late-Uruk administrative recording and authentication used several clay-based practices and devices rather than one uniform recording medium.
records.time_scope: Late Uruk, especially the late fourth millennium BCE
records.place_scope: Southern Mesopotamia and associated Late-Uruk administrative contexts
boundaries: Parallel practices must not be converted into a single mandatory developmental sequence.

world.operation: materialize numerical information through clay counting and recording practices
world.context: late prehistoric to Late-Uruk recording practices relevant to early Mesopotamian writing

records.statement: Numerical systems provide the strongest supported continuity between some pre-writing clay practices and proto-cuneiform, without implying a universal token code or one-to-one inheritance of every sign form.
records.time_scope: Late prehistoric to Late Uruk transition
records.place_scope: Mesopotamian and related archaeological contexts in the approved source set
boundaries: Neolithic clay objects must not be treated as a millennia-long standardized accounting code.
Continuity of individual non-numerical sign shapes requires separate support.

carries: on some examples exterior impressions or sealings
constrains: enclosed counters are not directly inspectable while the envelope remains closed

records.statement: Some hollow clay envelopes enclosed counters, and some also carried exterior impressions or sealings.

source_refs.locator: pp. 33–50; tokens, envelopes, sealings and numerical tablets

records.place_scope: Late-Uruk administrative contexts represented in the approved source set
boundaries: Exterior impressions are not universal to every envelope.
The affordance does not establish a single transitional step toward tablets.

permits: place quantity information directly on a durable exterior surface
carries: on some examples sealing or authentication marks

records.statement: Numerical tablets could carry quantity information directly as impressions on a durable clay surface, sometimes alongside authentication marks.

source_refs.locator: pp. 33–50; accounting systems and catalogue examples

records.place_scope: Southern Mesopotamia and related Late-Uruk administrative sites in the approved source set
boundaries: A numerical tablet alone does not identify a commodity, transaction mechanism or named actor.
Direct surface recording must not be described as wholesale replacement of envelopes or tokens.

world.relation: coexisted as overlapping recording and authentication practices
world.temporal_scope: formation period around the late fourth millennium BCE
world.qualification: overlap does not establish the exact contribution or replacement order of each practice

records.statement: Tokens, envelopes, sealings, numerical tablets and early written tablets belonged to overlapping practices rather than a securely demonstrated single replacement genealogy.
records.time_scope: Formation period around the late fourth millennium BCE
records.place_scope: Mesopotamian recording traditions in the approved research
boundaries: Temporal overlap must not be narrated as a deterministic evolutionary ladder.

world.left: growth in administrative and institutional scale
world.relation: co-occurred with and created pressure compatible with
world.right: greater demand for records and authentication
world.qualification: co-occurrence does not establish a sole cause or one-way causal sequence

records.statement: Administrative and institutional growth coincided with strong pressure for records and authentication without establishing administration as the sole cause of writing.
records.place_scope: Urban and institutional contexts in southern Mesopotamia represented in the approved sources
boundaries: Administration is a major formation pressure, not a monocausal explanation.

world.dimension: physical placement and inspectability of numerical information
world.earlier_state: quantities and authentication were handled across several coexisting physical devices and clay practices
world.later_state: numerical information increasingly appeared directly on durable clay surfaces, sometimes alongside authentication marks
world.coexistence: older and parallel clay practices continued to overlap with direct surface recording
world.qualification: the shift does not identify one invention event or an immediate complete replacement

records.statement: Within Late-Uruk recording practice, numerical information increasingly appeared directly on durable clay surfaces while older and parallel practices continued to coexist.
records.time_scope: Late Uruk, late fourth millennium BCE
records.place_scope: Southern Mesopotamia and related Late-Uruk administrative contexts
boundaries: Increasing direct surface recording does not imply immediate or complete replacement of other clay practices.

world.relation: may have formed a feedback relationship with
world.right: record systems that increased institutional capacity
world.qualification: medium-confidence model; later capacity effects cannot be back-projected as settled Late-Uruk fact

records.statement: A feedback relationship between expanding institutions and improved record systems is plausible but not established as a completed causal verdict.
records.place_scope: Institutional contexts represented in the approved sources
boundaries: Do not back-project later institutional effects as established Late-Uruk facts.

world.object: broken clay envelope OIM A64678 from Chogha Mish
permits: enclose small clay counters/tokens inside a hollow clay shell
carries: clay tokens still surviving inside the broken shell

records.statement: Catalogue object OIM A64678 is a Late-Uruk broken clay envelope from Chogha Mish with clay tokens still inside.
boundaries: This specimen does not identify a transaction, operator, motive or universal bulla function.
Do not treat it as an earlier step in a direct sequence leading to ChM III-937a.

world.object: sealed numerical-tablet fragment ChM III-937a from Chogha Mish
permits: carry numerical information directly as signs on a clay surface
carries: several animal seal rollings including a bull

records.statement: Catalogue object ChM III-937a is a Late-Uruk clay tablet fragment from Chogha Mish with five numeral signs and several animal seal rollings.
boundaries: The object does not identify the recorded commodity, transaction, operator or complete reading of the numerals.
Sharing a site and broad period with OIM A64678 does not establish a direct sequence or shared transaction type.

world.operation: shape damp clay and press or incise marks before the clay dries
world.result: numerical impressions or incised marks remain on the clay surface

records.statement: Artifact traces support a bounded reconstruction of an unknown record-maker shaping damp clay and creating marks before drying.

source_refs.locator: pp. 45–50; accounting devices and numerical tablets

records.place_scope: Southern Mesopotamia and related Late-Uruk recording contexts
boundaries: This is a manufacture/action reconstruction from object traces, not a witnessed event.

Named identities, motives, dialogue and emotions are not documented by the traces. Writer may create a plausible anonymous/composite scene under the creative brief, identified as reconstruction rather than artifact evidence.

participants: unidentified people involved in recording grain movements
world.operation: record grain deliveries and distributions, according to the likely interpretation of tablet 1988.433.2
information_or_relation_handled: barley and emmer grain movements, interpreted as probable deliveries/distributions
world.context: Early writing: Jemdet Nasr, ca. 3100–2900 BCE; probably Uruk. A bounded example, not a reconstruction of earlier Chogha Mish practice.

records.statement: Met tablet 1988.433.2, dated ca. 3100–2900 BCE and probably from Uruk, is interpreted as likely recording grain deliveries and distributions, including barley and emmer.

source_refs.locator: Object overview and Artwork Details, accession 1988.433.2

records.place_scope: Mesopotamia, probably Uruk; secure excavation context not asserted
boundaries: Keep the likely grain-delivery/distribution reading and probable findspot qualified.
This early-writing example does not establish an earlier Late-Uruk cause, a direct developmental sequence, or the use of the Chogha Mish objects.

Recipients, quantities, motives and individual outcomes are not established historical facts here. A signaled fictional illustration may add plausible human detail, but must not assert a known transaction, tax, wage or entitlement or prove a causal claim.

world.operation: record beer issued to workers as part of daily rations, in the British Museum interpretation of tablet 1989,0130.4
object_or_medium: signs shaped as pointed-base jars with wavy contents
a bowl directed toward a human head, interpreted as to eat and indicating rations
world.context: Southern Iraq, ca. 3100–3000 BCE, Late Uruk; precise excavated findspot and issuing institution are not established here.

records.statement: British Museum interprets tablet 1989,0130.4, dated ca. 3100–3000 BCE in southern Iraq, as recording beer issued to workers within daily rations. Its signs include pointed-base jars with wavy contents and a bowl toward a human head, interpreted as to eat and indicating rations.

source_refs.locator: Opening description, signs for beer and to eat, and object details

records.place_scope: Southern Iraq; specific Uruk findspot not asserted
boundaries: Retain the museum-attributed reading of daily worker beer rations. Do not present a named recipient, ration quantity, wage rate, issuer, coercion or deprivation outcome as established by this tablet. Identified fictional illustration remains available under the creative brief and cannot prove a historical consequence.
A recorded ration is not evidence that writing created that ration, guaranteed receipt, or first made distribution possible.
Do not identify this purchased object with the temple archives mentioned generally in the same essay or with the Chogha Mish and Met grain objects.

participants: people handling accounts and disbursements for large temple estates
specialist occupations including potters and metalworkers named in early Uruk lists
world.operation: keep economic records in an urban setting with temple estates and differentiated work
world.context: Uruk in the later fourth millennium BCE; general setting from Ira Spar, The Met, 2004.

records.statement: In late-fourth-millennium Uruk, large temple estates handled accounting and disbursement, and early written lists name specialist occupations including potters and metalworkers. These provide a concrete institutional and occupational setting for record-making.

source_refs.locator: Opening paragraphs on Uruk, temple estates and occupations

boundaries: Urban and temple accounting context does not establish a sole cause of writing or prove that all work, resources or records were temple-controlled.
Do not identify the workers in tablet 1989,0130.4 as potters, metalworkers or employees of a particular temple; these are separate contextual facts.

participants: people discarding early tablets from large temples
world.operation: reuse discarded early Uruk tablets as packing in foundations of new buildings
object_or_medium: clay tablets previously used as records
world.result: written clay surfaces occur in a secondary construction context rather than an intact working archive

records.statement: The British Museum account describes early Uruk tablets discarded from large temples and subsequently reused as packing in foundations of new buildings. This is a general account of secondary use, not the find history of tablet 1989,0130.4.

source_refs.locator: Final paragraph on early Uruk tablets and secondary building use

records.time_scope: Early Uruk tablets and subsequent ancient reuse; exact rebuilding date not supplied
records.place_scope: Uruk early-tablet contexts discussed generally by British Museum, not the findspot of 1989,0130.4
boundaries: Do not claim the purchased beer tablet was excavated from these foundations, or that every early tablet had this history.
No disaster, deliberate erasure, motive for disposal or named excavator is established. Later reading of the records does not imply their creators intended to address future generations.

constraints.rule: Do not convert overlapping clay practices into a direct token-to-tablet replacement genealogy.
Do not turn administrative pressure or institutional co-occurrence into a sole-cause or one-way causal verdict.
Do not label a specific economic mechanism such as market exchange, tax, tribute, redistribution, labor obligation or ownership unless independent transaction evidence supports it.
